summary:
The wave of fires in the Republic of Tunisia began on 1 June 2026, but reached a sharp peak from 12 July 2026 onward, continuing to the time of writing, coinciding with an exceptional heatwave in which temperatures reached close to 50°C in several governorates — including Kairouan, Jendouba, Gabès, Tozeur and Béja — while temperatures in the south-west reached around 49°C due to the hot, dry "Chehili" desert winds, according to the National Institute of Meteorology. The heatwave has been accompanied by strong winds and severe drought, triggering a wide series of forest and agricultural land fires, particularly in the mountainous and forested areas of the north and north-west of the country.

According to the latest official update, the total forest and agricultural area damaged by fire since the outbreak began has risen to around 12,000 hectares — a marked increase compared to earlier estimates of only 4,400 hectares as of 23 July 2026 (compared to 2,705 hectares over the same period in 2025) — reflecting the continued spread and intensification of the fires alongside the ongoing heatwave. Civil Protection also reported more than 35 forest fires between 1 June and 25 July 2026, while statistics show that forest areas damaged by fire over the past ten years totalled around 70,000 hectares (an annual average of about 7,000 hectares), underscoring the severity of the current season compared to the historical average. The Director General of Forests, Mohamed Naoufel Ben Haha, confirmed that the fires mainly affected cork-oak and Aleppo pine forests of significant social and economic importance to local forest communities, and that the situation in Le Kef governorate still requires continuous field vigilance.

Among the most significant fires recorded, by way of illustration and not an exhaustive list: the Ghar El Melh and Rafraf fire in Bizerte governorate (around 300 hectares); the Cap Negro fire in the Nefza delegation of Béja governorate (around 300 hectares); the Saqiyat Sidi Youssef fire in Le Kef governorate, which burned around 2,000 hectares and whose effects are still being dealt with; a fire in the Zaghouan mountains (Jebel Chahma area) affecting around 1,300 hectares of forest and farmland; along with scattered fires in Jendouba (Ain Draham), Nabeul (Rafraf, Jebel Nadhour), Siliana, Sfax, Gafsa, Kebili, Mahdia, Tozeur, Kasserine, Sidi Bouzid, Manouba and Tunis. Given the continued evolution of the fires and their expanding geographic scope, a detailed, reliable breakdown of the areas damaged by governorate is no longer available at this stage; the adopted cumulative figure remains 12,000 hectares to date, and the detailed regional breakdown will be updated later in coordination with the Directorate General of Forests.

The fires have also destroyed large numbers of fruit trees and hundreds of species of medicinal, cosmetic and aromatic herbs that thousands of residents in and around forested areas rely on gathering and selling as a primary or supplementary source of income, directly harming the livelihoods of these groups and deepening their economic vulnerability.

Firefighting operations have also become more difficult due to the rugged, mountainous terrain in many of the affected areas, the highly flammable nature of certain tree species such as Aleppo pine, and the continuing drought combined with the hot, dry "Chehili" winds — factors that together complicate the work of firefighting teams and increase the risk of fires reigniting and spreading further.

In terms of intervention frequency, Civil Protection units recorded hundreds of interventions per day in recent days; within just 48 hours, close to 2,800 interventions were logged, covering around 600 fires (roughly one fire every 5 minutes), while 900 fires were recorded over 72 hours between 20 and 22 July, and 296 fires were recorded among 939 interventions within a single 24-hour period. The Directorate General of Forests, for its part, took part in 917 firefighting operations since the start of the season, compared to only 620 operations over the same period in 2025.

The fires led to emergency evacuations of the population in several threatened areas (particularly in Bizerte and Jendouba), precautionary evacuation of sheep and livestock in the Siliana and Ain Draham areas, and material damage affecting a number of homes, wooden cabins, restaurants and beachfront tourist facilities in Bizerte (specifically Ghar El Melh and Rafraf), with no human casualties reported in official data as of the preparation of this document,except cases of smoke inhalation or limited skin burning .Based on the field assessment carried out by the Tunisian Red Crescent, the number of families affected by the electricity and water cuts accompanying the heatwave is 1,183.
